adhikaram.english: Conduct in the Presence of the King

kurals.tamil:
அகலாது அணுகாது தீக்காய்வார் போல்க
இகல்வேந்தர்ச் சேர்ந்தொழுகு வார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Akalaadhu anukaadhu theekkaaivaar polka
Ikalvendharch serndhozhuku vaar.
kurals.meaning: Those who serve changeable, powerful kings should behave like people warming themselves at a fire: never moving too far away, never coming too close.
kurals.elementary: On a cold night you sit near a campfire. Too far away and you shiver; too close and you get burned. Being around a very powerful person is the same: stay close enough to be useful, but never so close that you get burned.
kurals.university: The chapter opens the Kural’s treatment of how the minister or courtier (the Amaichiyal section) is to conduct himself with the ruler, and its governing image is the fire (thee) at which one warms oneself (theekkaaivaar). The paired negatives akalaadhu (not withdrawing) and anukaadhu (not approaching) define a calibrated middle distance rather than a fixed rule. Parimelazhagar reads ikalvendhar as kings whose temper easily turns to hostility (ikal = enmity, variance), so the danger is not the king’s wickedness but his volatility: the same fire that warms can burn. The simile closely parallels Kautilya (Arthashastra 5.4), who likens royal service to life in fire, and Dhaumya’s counsel in the Mahabharata that the king is a great fire. The traditional sandhi text reads “அகலா தணுகாது” and “விகல்வேந்தர்”, which divide into the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “To dwell with a king is, alas, difficult. ... the king, who is a deity in an embodied form, is as a great fire sanctified with all the mantras.”
hinduism.explanation: Before the Pandavas go into hiding as servants at King Virata’s court, the priest Dhaumya warns them that living near a king is hard, and he compares the king to a great sacred fire.
hinduism.tie_back: Dhaumya and Valluvar use the same image, the king as a fire, to teach the same thing: approach carefully.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Virata Parva, Section 4 (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close parallel. Both texts compare the king to a fire, although Dhaumya’s fire is sacred and Valluvar’s is a hearth fire for warming.

christianity.quote_or_event: “When thou art bidden of any man to a wedding, sit not down in the highest room; lest a more honourable man than thou be bidden of him ... But when thou art bidden, go and sit down in the lowest room; that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells guests not to grab the seat nearest the host, because they may be moved down in shame. It is better to be invited closer.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it teaches that pushing too close to the powerful backfires, and that the right nearness is the one you are invited to.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the warning against coming too near, but Luke says nothing about the opposite danger of staying too far away.

islam.quote_or_event: “He who lives in the desert will become rude; he who pursues the game will be negligent, and he who visits a king will be perverted.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that going to the court of a ruler puts a person’s integrity at risk, because being near power tempts and tests people.
islam.tie_back: The hadith names the burn that the Kural’s fire image warns about: getting too close to rulers is dangerous.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 2859 (graded sahih by al-Albani)
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on the danger of nearness. The hadith leans toward avoiding the ruler, while the Kural assumes the minister must serve him.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Be careful [in your dealings] with the ruling authorities for they do not befriend a person except for their own needs; they seem like friends when it is to their own interest, but they do not stand by a man in the hour of his distress.”
judaism.explanation: Rabban Gamaliel warns that rulers act friendly when it helps them and drop you when it does not, so deal with them warily.
judaism.tie_back: This is the same careful middle distance the Kural asks for. Rulers can be useful, but you cannot safely get close to them.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close in spirit. Both are prudent rules for dealing with fickle power; the Mishnah stresses the ruler’s self-interest, the Kural his volatility.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let him prudently keep not too far from the king nor yet too near to him, and let him stand ready before him, telling something for his lord to hear.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Vidhurapandita Jataka, the wise minister Vidhura teaches his family the rules for living at a king’s court, and this is one of them.
buddhism.tie_back: This is nearly the Kural’s own wording: not too far and not too near.
buddhism.source: Vidhurapandita Jataka (Ja 545), v. 154, The King’s Court (Rājavasati) section
buddhism._accuracy_note: Almost word for word. The Jataka leaves out the fire image but gives the same neither-far-nor-near rule.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Daedalus fits wings to his son Icarus and tells him to fly a middle course: too low and the sea spray will soak the feathers, too high and the sun will melt the wax. Icarus, excited, soars toward the sun and falls into the sea.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows that safety lies in a middle distance, and that being carried too close to a blazing power ends in disaster.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Icarus flying at the sun is the mythic version of the courtier who comes too near the fire.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Same structure: the middle path between two dangers, with fire or the sun as the danger of nearness. Ovid’s story is not about serving a king.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Self-protection shall be the first and constant thought of a wise man; for the life of a man under the service of a king is aptly compared to life in fire.”
philosophy.explanation: Kautilya ends his chapter on a courtier’s conduct by saying that serving a king is like living in fire. Fire burns only the body, but a king can ruin or raise a servant’s whole family.
philosophy.tie_back: Kautilya and Valluvar build their advice on the same metaphor of royal service as fire.
philosophy.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra 5.4, The Conduct of a Courtier (trans. R. Shamasastry)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Exact shared metaphor. Kautilya uses it to urge self-protection, not to measure distance, but the practical lesson is the same.

adhikaram.english: Conduct in the Presence of the King

kurals.tamil:
மன்னர் விழைப விழையாமை மன்னரால்
மன்னிய ஆக்கந் தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Mannar vizhaipa vizhaiyaamai mannaraal
Manniya aakkam tharum.
kurals.meaning: If you do not covet the things the king himself desires, the king will give you lasting prosperity.
kurals.elementary: Picture a class helper who never tries to grab the teacher’s special chair or the teacher’s favourite pen. Because the teacher never has to worry about that helper, the teacher trusts them more and more. Not wanting what belongs to the boss is how you earn lasting trust.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on the repeated root vizhai (to desire): the servant must not desire (vizhaiyaamai) what the kings desire (mannar vizhaipa). Parimelazhagar takes the objects to be the king’s own enjoyments, such as his ornaments, pleasures and women, which a courtier must never share or rival. Mu. Varadarasanar instead reads “those whom the king favours”, meaning one should not compete for the king’s favourites. Either way, the reward is manniya aakkam, prosperity that lasts (manniya = enduring), and it comes through the king himself (mannaraal). The play on mannar/manniya is typical of Valluvar’s sound patterning. The older text in thirukkural-thamizh.org reads மன்னரான் for மன்னரால், a dialectal instrumental ending with the same meaning.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bharata refuses the throne his mother schemed to win for him. He goes to the forest to bring back his brother Rama, and when Rama will not return he rules only as regent, with Rama’s sandals placed on the throne.
hinduism.explanation: Bharata will not claim anything that belongs to the rightful king, even when it is handed to him, and he is remembered with lasting honour for it.
hinduism.tie_back: Bharata shows the Kural’s rule in its purest form: he refuses to desire what is the king’s, and that refusal secures his enduring standing.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (Bharata and the padukas)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong moral parallel, but Bharata is a royal brother acting as regent, not a courtier serving a king.

christianity.quote_or_event: “When thou sittest to eat with a ruler, consider diligently what is before thee: And put a knife to thy throat, if thou be a man given to appetite. Be not desirous of his dainties: for they are deceitful meat.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb tells someone eating at a ruler’s table to hold back and not crave the ruler’s luxuries, because they are a trap.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts tell the courtier not to desire the ruler’s own delights.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close: do not covet the ruler’s things. Proverbs stresses the danger of craving, while the Kural stresses the reward for restraint.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not extend your eyes toward that by which We have given enjoyment to [some] categories of them, [its being but] the splendor of worldly life by which We test them. And the provision of your Lord is better and more enduring.”
islam.explanation: The Quran tells believers not to gaze longingly at the luxuries of the powerful, because those are a test. What God provides is better and lasts longer.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sets not coveting the splendour of the great against a more enduring reward.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on not coveting the luxuries of the powerful and on the ‘more enduring’ reward. In the Quran that reward comes from God, not from the king.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Love work, hate acting the superior, and do not attempt to draw near to the ruling authority.”
judaism.explanation: Shemaiah teaches that one should work honestly, dislike playing the lord, and not court the government.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Hate acting the superior’ is close to the Kural’s point: do not want the powers and pleasures that belong to the ruler.
judaism._accuracy_note: Partial match. Shemaiah advises keeping away from rulers entirely, while the Kural assumes you serve them and simply do not covet what is theirs.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let him on no account ever enjoy the same pleasures as the king, let him follow behind in everything, such a one may dwell in a king’s court.”
buddhism.explanation: Vidhura’s rules for courtiers forbid enjoying what the king enjoys. The courtier is always to stay a step behind the king.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s rule almost exactly: do not desire the king’s own pleasures.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near-verbatim parallel to Parimelazhagar’s reading. The Jataka does not spell out the reward of lasting wealth.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The courtier Damocles praised the wealth of the tyrant Dionysius of Syracuse, so Dionysius let him enjoy it for a day. Damocles sat among golden dishes and perfumes, but a sword hung above his head by a single horsehair, and he soon begged to leave.
greek_mythology.explanation: The courtier envied his ruler’s luxury, was given a taste of it, and found out what danger came with it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural tells the servant not to desire the king’s things. Damocles is the classic courtier who did, and learned why.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Direct story of a courtier coveting a ruler’s pleasures. The point is the danger of power rather than the reward for restraint, and the tale is Greek history told by Cicero, not myth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus says that an invitation to a great man’s dinner is sold at a price, namely flattery and attendance. If you are unwilling to pay it, you should not complain about going without the dinner, because you still have not had to flatter.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic teaches that the privileges of the powerful always come with a price, and that a free person can simply decline to want them.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Epictetus asks us to stop wanting the great man’s goods, although for him the reward is inner freedom rather than royal favour.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Shares the idea of not desiring what the powerful enjoy. The motive is different: Stoic independence, not service.

adhikaram.english: Conduct in the Presence of the King

kurals.tamil:
போற்றின் அரியவை போற்றல் கடுத்தபின்
தேற்றுதல் யார்க்கும் அரிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Potrin ariyavai potral kaduththapin
Thetrudhal yaarkkum aridhu.
kurals.meaning: If you want to protect yourself, guard against grave faults, because once the king grows suspicious, no one can set his mind at rest again.
kurals.elementary: A glass vase with a crack can be glued, but you can always see the crack. Trust works the same way. It is much easier to be careful and never break it than to try to fix it after someone starts to doubt you.
kurals.university: The first line plays on potru (to guard, to preserve): potrin (if you would guard [yourself]) and potral (guard against). Ariyavai are, in Parimelazhagar’s gloss, grave faults the king will find hard to pardon. The key word is kaduththal, to suspect or to be incensed, and the second line states the psychology bluntly: once suspicion has formed, thetrudhal (reassuring or convincing) is difficult for anyone (yaarkkum). The Kural’s wider theory of trust helps here. Chapter 51 (Therindhu Thelidhal) warns the king against doubting a servant he has tested, so this couplet gives the courtier’s side of the same danger. The sandhi text in older editions runs “போற்றி னரியவை” and “றேற்றுதல் யார்க்கு மரிது.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Panchatantra’s first book, the jackal Damanaka poisons the friendship between the lion-king Pingalaka and his trusted minister, the bull Sanjivaka, by whispering suspicions to each of them. Once the lion suspects the bull, nothing can undo it, and Sanjivaka is killed.
hinduism.explanation: The frame story of ‘The Loss of Friends’ shows how quickly a ruler’s suspicion, once planted, destroys even a favoured servant.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s warning played out: after suspicion arises, reassurance is almost impossible.
hinduism.source: Panchatantra, Book I (Mitrabheda), frame story of Pingalaka and Sanjivaka
hinduism._accuracy_note: Powerful illustration of how suspicion cannot be undone. In the fable the suspicion is planted by a slanderer, not caused by the servant’s own fault.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then the presidents and princes sought to find occasion against Daniel concerning the kingdom; but they could find none occasion nor fault; forasmuch as he was faithful, neither was there any error or fault found in him.”
christianity.explanation: At the Persian court, Daniel’s jealous rivals search for a fault to use against him and cannot find one, because he has been careful and faithful.
christianity.tie_back: Daniel lives out the Kural’s first line: guard against faults so that suspicion has nothing to hold on to.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on avoiding faults that invite suspicion. Daniel’s danger comes from his rivals, not from the king’s own doubts.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the king said, ‘Bring him to me.’ But when the messenger came to him, [Joseph] said, ‘Return to your master and ask him what is the case of the women who cut their hands. Indeed, my Lord is Knowing of their plan.’”
islam.explanation: Joseph has been imprisoned under suspicion. When the king summons him, he refuses to leave until the king has formally investigated the accusation and cleared his name.
islam.tie_back: Joseph knows the Kural’s truth: suspicion at court does not fade by itself, so a full clearing is needed before he can safely serve.
islam._accuracy_note: Shows how hard suspicion is to lift. Joseph was innocent, while the Kural is about avoiding real faults.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If the spirit of the ruler rise up against thee, leave not thy place; for yielding pacifieth great offences.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet advises that when a ruler turns angry with you, you should stay calm at your post and yield, because only calm submission soothes great offences.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts see how hard it is to recover once a ruler’s mind turns against you. Kohelet gives the remedy, the Kural the prevention.
judaism._accuracy_note: Shares the setting of a ruler turned hostile. Kohelet is more hopeful that yielding can calm him than the Kural, which says reassurance is hard for anyone.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let not the wise man, thinking himself to be held in honour, ever venture to speak roughly to the suspicious king.”
buddhism.explanation: Vidhura warns that kings are naturally suspicious, so a courtier must never give offence, even when he feels secure.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts treat the king’s suspicion as a hazard that the courtier must avoid provoking in the first place.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the idea of the suspicious king and the need for caution. It does not state that suspicion, once raised, cannot be cured.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the court of King Proetus, the queen falsely accuses the young hero Bellerophon. Proetus believes her and sends Bellerophon away with a sealed tablet asking the king of Lycia to kill him. Bellerophon has to survive monsters and ambushes before he is trusted again.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s story shows how a single suspicion at court can turn a king against a guest and set off a long ordeal.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Proetus’s suspicion, once formed, could not be talked away, which is exactly the Kural’s warning.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates how durable a king’s suspicion is, but Bellerophon was innocent, whereas the Kural concerns real faults.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca tells of a man who had grown old in the service of kings. Asked how he had managed something so rare at court, he replied that it was by accepting injuries and thanking the king for them.
philosophy.explanation: The Roman Stoic uses the anecdote to show how precarious life at a royal court is, where one misstep or show of resentment can be fatal.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts assume that a ruler’s displeasure, once aroused, is almost impossible to undo, so survival means never provoking it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Captures the precariousness of court life. Seneca’s focus is on hiding anger, not on avoiding faults.

adhikaram.english: Conduct in the Presence of the King

kurals.tamil:
செவிச்சொல்லும் சேர்ந்த நகையும் அவித்தொழுகல்
ஆன்ற பெரியா ரகத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Sevichchollum serndha nakaiyum aviththozhukal
Aandra periyaar akaththu.
kurals.meaning: In the presence of great and powerful people, do not whisper in anyone’s ear or share a private smile with someone else.
kurals.elementary: Imagine you are speaking to the class and two children in the front row start whispering and giggling. You would wonder whether they were laughing at you. That is why, around important people, you should not whisper or trade secret smiles.
kurals.university: Sevichchol is literally ‘ear-speech’, words whispered into another person’s ear, and serndha nakai is ‘joined laughter’, a smile or glance shared with someone else. Solomon Pappaiah glosses it as winking and smiling while looking at another’s face. The verb avi (to extinguish or suppress) asks the courtier to put out these impulses altogether. Aandra periyaar are ‘the great ones who are complete in power’, which Parimelazhagar takes as kings. The rule rests on the suspicion theme of the previous couplet: private signals between courtiers look to a ruler like conspiracy or mockery. Kautilya’s Arthashastra 5.4 lists almost the same prohibitions, secret talk with another in the assembly and loud laughter without cause. The older text reads “செவிச்சொல்லுஞ் சேர்ந்த நகையு மவித்தொழுக / லான்ற பெரியா ரகத்து.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: “In the presence of even laughable objects, a man should not break out into loud laughter, like a maniac; nor should one show (unreasonable) gravity by containing himself, to the utmost. One should smile modestly, to show his interest.”
hinduism.explanation: Dhaumya teaches the Pandavas to control their laughter at court: neither laughing wildly nor standing stiff, but smiling modestly.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts treat uncontrolled laughter in the ruler’s presence as a breach of the courtier’s discipline.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Virata Parva, Section 4 (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the laughter half of the Kural. Dhaumya does not mention whispering, and he allows a modest smile.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Being filled with all unrighteousness, fornication, wickedness, covetousness, maliciousness; full of envy, murder, debate, deceit, malignity; whisperers,”
christianity.explanation: Paul lists ‘whisperers’, people who spread talk behind others’ backs, among the vices of a corrupt society.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural bans ear-whispering before great persons, and Paul counts whispering itself as a vice.
christianity._accuracy_note: Weak match. Paul condemns whispering as gossip in general, not as a breach of court etiquette.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, when you converse privately, do not converse about sin and aggression and disobedience to the Messenger but converse about righteousness and piety.”
islam.explanation: Surah al-Mujadila addresses the private conversations (najwa) that some people held in the Prophet’s community, which hurt others and bred suspicion.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Quran treats private whispering in the leader’s circle as a source of harm and mistrust.
islam._accuracy_note: Good thematic match on whispering within a leader’s community. The Quran regulates its content rather than banning it outright.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Curse not the king, no not in thy thought; and curse not the rich in thy bedchamber: for a bird of the air shall carry the voice, and that which hath wings shall tell the matter.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet warns that even private talk about the king has a way of reaching him.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural forbids whispers in the king’s presence because whispers always look suspicious and seldom stay secret.
judaism._accuracy_note: Shares the idea that private words about rulers are dangerous. Kohelet is about speech behind the king’s back, not etiquette in front of him.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let him not laugh too much, nor keep always silent; he should utter, when the due season comes, a concise and measured speech.”
buddhism.explanation: Vidhura teaches that a courtier should keep his laughter and speech measured.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts ask the servant to rein in laughter and loose talk before the king.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches the restraint on laughter. The Jataka does not mention whispering or shared smiles with others.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas’s barber discovers that Apollo has given the king ass’s ears. Unable to keep the secret, he whispers it into a hole in the ground, but the reeds that grow there murmur it to everyone.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s story shows that whispered words about a king do not stay hidden.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural forbids ear-whispering at court. Midas’s barber shows why: whispers about the powerful always travel.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates the danger of whispering about a ruler. It is not about behaviour in the ruler’s presence.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He shall also avoid talking to another in secret, mutual conversation with another in the assembly (of ministers) ... nor loud laughter with no cause for jest.”
philosophy.explanation: Kautilya lists behaviours a courtier must avoid in the king’s assembly, including whispered side-conversations and laughter without cause.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural’s pair: whispering to another and laughing with another before the king.
philosophy.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra 5.4, The Conduct of a Courtier (trans. R. Shamasastry)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near-exact parallel. Both texts name secret talk and shared laughter as forbidden in the royal presence.

adhikaram.english: Conduct in the Presence of the King

kurals.tamil:
எப்பொருளும் ஓரார் தொடரார்மற் றப்பொருளை
விட்டக்கால் கேட்க மறை.
kurals.transliteration:
Epporulum oraar thodaraarmatru apporulai
Vittakkaal ketka marai.
kurals.meaning: When the king speaks in secret, do not strain to overhear anything or press him with questions. Hear the secret only if he chooses to tell you.
kurals.elementary: When your parents are talking quietly in the kitchen, it is tempting to sneak up and listen, or to keep asking ‘What were you talking about?’ The polite and trustworthy thing is to wait. If they want you to know, they will tell you.
kurals.university: The couplet sets out three stages. Oraar means not listening intently or eavesdropping (oru = to attend closely). Thodaraar means not following up with questions. Vittakkaal ketka means listening only once the king himself lets the matter out. The final word, marai (secret, hidden counsel), is held back to the end, which gives the line a sense of withheld information. Parimelazhagar sets the scene as a king in secret counsel with others, and the logic follows from 693: curiosity about royal secrets is exactly what breeds suspicion. The joined text in older editions reads “எப்பொருளு மோரார் தொடரார்மற் றப்பொருளை / விட்டக்காற் கேட்க மறை.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: “No one should keep contact with royal secrets.”
hinduism.explanation: Dhaumya tells the Pandavas that, living at Virata’s court, they must keep clear of the king’s secrets and later never disclose them.
hinduism.tie_back: Dhaumya and Valluvar both make keeping away from royal secrets a basic rule of survival at court.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Virata Parva, Section 4 (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Direct match on royal secrets. It lacks the Kural’s stages of not overhearing, not asking, and hearing only when told.

christianity.quote_or_event: “It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power.”
christianity.explanation: When the disciples press the risen Jesus about when the kingdom will be restored, he tells them that some things are kept by the Father and are not theirs to demand.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, the one who holds authority also decides what to reveal, and the follower should not pry.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the principle of not pressing a sovereign for reserved knowledge. The setting is theological, not political.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, avoid much [negative] assumption. Indeed, some assumption is sin. And do not spy or backbite each other.”
islam.explanation: The Quran forbids spying (tajassus), prying into matters others have not chosen to share.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s ban on overhearing and interrogating is a court-specific form of this general rule against spying.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on the ethic of not prying. The Quran addresses everyone, not only a courtier and his king.

judaism.quote_or_event: “It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs says that concealing is God’s prerogative and investigating belongs to the king, so knowledge and secrecy are part of sovereign authority.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural treats the king’s marai (secret) as his to keep or reveal, and Proverbs likewise puts the right to conceal and search with the sovereign.
judaism._accuracy_note: Weak but real parallel about sovereigns and hidden things. It does not directly forbid courtiers from prying.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “When the king finds out his moral qualities, his wisdom and his purity of heart, then he learns to trust him and hides not his secrets from him.”
buddhism.explanation: Vidhura teaches that a courtier comes to share the king’s secrets only when the king chooses to share them, after his character has been proved.
buddhism.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s final clause: the secret should reach you because the king lets it go, not because you took it.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Complementary angle: secrets are given as trust grows. It does not explicitly forbid eavesdropping.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The hunter Actaeon strays into the goddess Diana’s hidden grotto and sees her bathing. For seeing what was not meant for him, he is turned into a stag and torn apart by his own hounds.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid tells the story as a warning about the terrible cost of intruding on what the powerful keep hidden.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural warns against overhearing a sovereign’s secret, and Actaeon is the mythic example of the price of seeing what is reserved.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Actaeon’s intrusion was accidental rather than curious prying. Ovid himself says the fault was chance, not crime.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “‘Which one of my possessions may I share with you?’ ‘Anything, Sire,’ said Philippides, ‘except your secrets.’”
philosophy.explanation: In his essay on curiosity, Plutarch praises the comic poet Philippides, who asked King Lysimachus for any gift except his secrets. Plutarch adds that people who pry into the affairs of the more powerful destroy themselves.
philosophy.tie_back: Philippides is the ideal courtier of this Kural: he positively does not want to know the king’s secrets.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, On Being a Busybody (De curiositate) 4, Moralia 517 (Loeb trans. W. C. Helmbold)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Excellent parallel on courtiers and royal secrets. Plutarch’s motive is prudence against curiosity, much like Valluvar’s.

adhikaram.english: Conduct in the Presence of the King

kurals.tamil:
குறிப்பறிந்து காலங் கருதி வெறுப்பில
வேண்டுப வேட்பச் சொலல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kurippu arindhu kaalam karudhi veruppila
Venduba vetpach cholal.
kurals.meaning: Read the king’s mood, wait for the right moment, and then say what is needed and not displeasing, in a way he will want to hear.
kurals.elementary: If you want to ask for a later bedtime, you would not ask when Mum is rushing or cross. You would wait until she is relaxed, ask kindly, and explain why it is a good idea. Choosing the right moment and the right words makes people ready to listen.
kurals.university: The couplet lays out three steps. Kurippu arindhu means reading the ruler’s inner disposition from outward signs, the subject of the very next chapter (71, Kurippu Arithal). Kaalam karudhi means weighing the right time, echoing chapter 49 (Kaalam Arithal). Then comes the manner of speech: veruppila (things not repugnant) and venduba (things needed or useful), spoken vetpa (so that he desires to hear them). Parimelazhagar notes that what is needful must still be said, but framed so that it is welcome. That makes this not flattery but an art of timing and packaging, close to what Greek rhetoric called kairos. The traditional text is the same apart from sandhi.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him say what is true, let him say what is pleasing, let him utter no disagreeable truth, and let him utter no agreeable falsehood; that is the eternal law.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu sets the rule for virtuous speech: it should be both true and pleasant, avoiding harsh truths and sweet lies alike.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar’s ‘needed and not displeasing, said so he wants to hear it’ is a court-specific form of Manu’s true-and-pleasing ideal.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close on pleasing but proper speech. Manu does not mention reading signs or timing, and his ban on disagreeable truths goes further than the Kural.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks that speech always be gracious and well-seasoned, fitted to each listener.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts value truth delivered gracefully and fitted to the listener.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the gracious-speech element. It lacks the emphasis on reading the king’s mood and timing.

islam.quote_or_event: “And speak to him with gentle speech that perhaps he may be reminded or fear [Allah].”
islam.explanation: God sends Moses and Aaron to Pharaoh, the most powerful and hostile king of their time, and tells them to speak gently so that their message might be received.
islam.tie_back: Even a hard truth to a king should be spoken so that he can hear it, which is the Kural’s ‘so he desires to hear’.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on gentle framing of a needed message to a ruler. Moses is a prophet confronting Pharaoh, not a minister serving him.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And I said unto the king, If it please the king, and if thy servant have found favour in thy sight, that thou wouldest send me unto Judah, unto the city of my fathers’ sepulchres, that I may build it.”
judaism.explanation: Nehemiah, cupbearer to the Persian king, waits until the king notices his sad face and asks what he wants. He silently prays, then makes his request in carefully courteous terms, and it is granted.
judaism.tie_back: Nehemiah reads the moment, waits for the opening, and frames a needed request pleasingly, which is the Kural’s method exactly.
judaism._accuracy_note: Excellent narrative parallel: timing, reading the king, courteous framing and success. It is a single episode rather than a stated rule.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In the case of words that the Tathagata knows to be factual, true, beneficial, and endearing & agreeable to others, he has a sense of the proper time for saying them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Prince Abhaya that even true, beneficial and pleasing words should be spoken only at the right time.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha’s three tests of true, beneficial and timely match the Kural’s needful, not displeasing, and at the right time.
buddhism.source: Abhaya Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 58 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close on beneficial speech and timing. The Buddha speaks to anyone, not specifically to a king.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Croesus, captured by Cyrus, first asks whether he may speak or must keep silent. Given leave, he points out that Cyrus’s soldiers are plundering what is now Cyrus’s own property and suggests a tactful remedy. Cyrus is pleased and adopts it.
greek_mythology.explanation: Herodotus shows a captive speaking to a conqueror: he asks permission, picks his moment, and offers advice framed around the king’s own interest.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Croesus uses the Kural’s full method of reading the moment and framing useful counsel so that the king wants to hear it.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close narrative parallel from Greek history. It is not mythology in the strict sense.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He, therefore, added one more to the number of those who have shown to their bitter cost how little kings care for their friends' good advice.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca tells how Praexaspes advised King Cambyses to drink less, and the drunken king shot the adviser's son through the heart to prove his hand was steady. Seneca judges that Praexaspes was wiser in holding his tongue afterwards than in offering correction to such a king in the first place.
philosophy.tie_back: The tale shows the danger the Kural guards against, which is giving a king sound but unwelcome advice without reading his mood or waiting for the right moment.
philosophy.source: Seneca, De Ira (Of Anger), III.14 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Wikisource (Stewart translation, Book III). Partial match: it is a cautionary example of ill-timed counsel to a king, not a positive teaching on timing and pleasing speech. Seneca's main concern in the chapter is controlling anger.

adhikaram.english: Conduct in the Presence of the King

kurals.tamil:
வேட்பன சொல்லி வினையில எஞ்ஞான்றும்
கேட்பினும் சொல்லா விடல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vetpana solli vinaiyila egngnaandrum
Ketpinum sollaa vidal.
kurals.meaning: Tell the king what is truly worth his wanting, and never speak of useless or harmful things, even if he himself asks for them.
kurals.elementary: If your friend asks you to help them copy homework, a good friend says no, even though the friend asked. A good helper suggests things that really help, and stays quiet about bad ideas, even when invited to share them.
kurals.university: Vetpana means ‘what is desirable’, which in Parimelazhagar’s reading are things beneficial to the king, not merely things he would like to hear. Vinaiyila means ‘what has no deed’, that is, fruitless or unprofitable matters. The concessive ketpinum (‘even if he asks’) is the moral centre of the couplet: the courtier’s integrity must hold even against a direct royal request, and egngnaandrum (at no time whatever) rules out exceptions. Commentators differ here. Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as ‘speak only what the king desires’, while Solomon Pappaiah reads ‘speak useful things even unasked’. Pope’s ‘speak pleasant things’ softens the point. The couplet thus protects 696 from being read as a licence to flatter. The older text reads “வினையில வெஞ்ஞான்றுங் / கேட்பினுஞ் சொல்லா விடல்.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A person should set forth before the king those topics that are both profitable and pleasant; but should a subject be profitable without being pleasant, he should still communicate it, despite its disagreeableness. ... and not to indulge in speech that is alike unpleasant and profitless.”
hinduism.explanation: Dhaumya ranks the courtier’s speech by usefulness. Say what is useful and pleasant, say what is useful even if unpleasant, and never say what is both unpleasant and useless.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Dhaumya makes benefit, not the king’s wish, the test of what a courtier should say.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Virata Parva, Section 4 (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close in its logic. Dhaumya does not add the Kural’s ‘even if he asks’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that empty, useless words carry moral weight and will be judged.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural bans useless speech even when the king asks for it. Jesus makes every idle word answerable before God.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the condemnation of useless speech. It is not about counsel to a ruler.

islam.quote_or_event: “Anybody who believes in Allah and the Last Day should talk what is good or keep quiet.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet makes useful, good speech or else silence a mark of faith.
islam.tie_back: Speak what is good or say nothing is the Kural’s rule, and the courtier follows it even before the king.
islam._accuracy_note: Good general match. It lacks the specific case of refusing a ruler who asks for useless counsel.

judaism.quote_or_event: “As the LORD liveth, what the LORD saith unto me, that will I speak.”
judaism.explanation: When King Ahab’s four hundred prophets all flatter him with promises of victory, the prophet Micaiah is told to agree with them. He refuses and speaks only the unwelcome truth.
judaism.tie_back: Micaiah refuses to say empty, harmful things even when the king’s court demands them, which is the Kural’s ‘even if he asks, do not say it’.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong parallel on refusing to tell a king what he wants to hear. Micaiah is a prophet, not a courtier, and his truth is blunt rather than pleasing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In the case of words that the Tathagata knows to be factual, true, unbeneficial, but endearing & agreeable to others, he does not say them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha will not say even true and pleasant things if they do no good.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha’s refusal of pleasing but useless speech is exactly the Kural’s refusal to say unprofitable things, whatever the king wants.
buddhism.source: Abhaya Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 58 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near-exact principle: benefit, not pleasure, decides speech.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “O Solon, our converse with kings should be either as rare, or as pleasing as is possible.” “No indeed!” said Solon, “but either as rare or as beneficial as possible.”
greek_mythology.explanation: At King Croesus’s court, the fable-writer Aesop advises Solon to speak to kings pleasantly or not at all. Solon corrects him: speak rarely, or speak what is truly beneficial.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This exchange sets 696 against 697. Aesop voices the ‘pleasing’ side, and Solon voices Valluvar’s final word: benefit over pleasure.
greek_mythology.source: Plutarch, Life of Solon 28 (trans. Bernadotte Perrin, Loeb)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Remarkably exact parallel. Solon’s ‘as beneficial as possible’ is Parimelazhagar’s reading of vetpana. This is Greek history, not myth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “When asked, he should tell the king what is both good and pleasing, but not what is bad though pleasing; if the king is pleased to listen, he may secretly tell what though unpleasant, is good.”
philosophy.explanation: Kautilya tells the courtier to offer what is good and pleasing, to refuse what is bad even if pleasing, and to say hard truths privately.
philosophy.tie_back: ‘Not what is bad though pleasing’ is the Kural’s refusal to speak unprofitable things even when asked.
philosophy.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra 5.4, The Conduct of a Courtier (trans. R. Shamasastry)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near-exact parallel. Kautilya adds private delivery of unpleasant truths, which the Kural does not mention.

adhikaram.english: Conduct in the Presence of the King

kurals.tamil:
இளையர் இனமுறையர் என்றிகழார் நின்ற
ஒளியோடு ஒழுகப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ilaiyar inamuraiyar endru ikazhaar nindra
Oliyodu ozhukap padum.
kurals.meaning: Do not look down on the king by thinking ‘he is younger than me’ or ‘he is my relative’. Behave in keeping with the dignity of the position he holds.
kurals.elementary: Suppose your older cousin becomes the team captain. At family dinners they are just your cousin, but on the field you listen to them as captain. The job deserves respect, whoever is doing it.
kurals.university: The couplet names two excuses for disrespect: ilaiyar (‘he is our junior’) and inamuraiyar (‘he stands in such-and-such a kinship relation to us’). Ikazhaar forbids the contempt that comes from both. The key phrase is nindra oli, ‘the radiance that abides [in him]’. Parimelazhagar interprets it as the divine light or majesty present in the king, and Pope accordingly translates ‘the glory kingly state doth bring’. Modern readers such as Solomon Pappaiah reduce it to respect for the office (padhavi) rather than the person. The idea that royal dignity belongs to the office, not the age or family of its holder, closely matches Manusmriti 7.8. The couplet is also a warning to royal kinsmen, whose familiarity is the most tempting route to contempt.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Even an infant king must not be despised, (from an idea) that he is a (mere) mortal; for he is a great deity in human form.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu teaches that a king’s youth is no reason to disrespect him, because kingship itself carries divine majesty.
hinduism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s own claim. ‘He is young’ is no excuse, because of the radiance (oli) that resides in the king.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-exact parallel on youth and the king’s divine radiance. Manu does not mention kinship.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the young church leader Timothy that his youth should not be used to discount his authority.
christianity.tie_back: Paul, like the Kural, rejects ‘he is young’ as a reason to despise someone who holds authority.
christianity._accuracy_note: Direct match on not despising youth in authority. It is addressed to the young leader rather than to those under him.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you.”
islam.explanation: The Quran commands obedience to those who hold rightful authority, grounding it in the office rather than personal qualities.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it directs respect to ‘those in authority’ as such, whatever their age or relation to us.
islam._accuracy_note: Supports respect for office generally. It does not address youth or kinship.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The LORD forbid that I should do this thing unto my master, the LORD’S anointed, to stretch forth mine hand against him, seeing he is the anointed of the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: David, hunted by King Saul, who is also his father-in-law, has the chance to kill him in a cave. He refuses because Saul still bears the anointing of kingship.
judaism.tie_back: David honours the anointing, the office’s sacred radiance, over his personal relationship and grievance, which is the Kural’s nindra oli.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong parallel on reverence for the office despite personal ties. The issue is violence, not casual contempt.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The king does not count as a common person, the king must not be paired with anyone else; kings are easily vexed, as the eye is hurt if touched by a barley-awn.”
buddhism.explanation: Vidhura warns courtiers never to treat the king as an equal or an ordinary man.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts forbid bringing the king down to one’s own level, whether as a junior or as family.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close on not treating the king as an equal. Youth and kinship are not named.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Achilles quarrels with Agamemnon, old Nestor tells him not to strive against a sceptred king. Achilles may be the stronger fighter and the son of a goddess, but the king whom Zeus has honoured holds the greater rank.
greek_mythology.explanation: Nestor argues that personal superiority in strength and birth does not cancel the honour that belongs to the king’s office.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural says the same: personal factors such as age or family do not outrank the dignity of the throne.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Clear parallel on the office outranking the person. Nestor speaks of strength and divine birth rather than youth and kinship.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Duties are universally measured by relations. … In this manner, therefore, you will find, from the idea of a neighbor, a citizen, a general, the corresponding duties if you accustom yourself to contemplate the several relations.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus teaches that what we owe someone follows from the role or relation in which they stand to us, such as father, brother, citizen or general, and not from what we think of them personally.
philosophy.tie_back: In the same way the Kural asks that the king be treated according to the office he holds, not according to his age or his kinship with oneself.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Carter translation). Partial match: the shared principle is that the role sets the duty. Epictetus does not discuss rulers who are younger than oneself or related to one, which is the Kural's specific case.

adhikaram.english: Conduct in the Presence of the King

kurals.tamil:
கொளப்பட்டேம் என்றெண்ணிக் கொள்ளாத செய்யார்
துளக்கற்ற காட்சி யவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kolappattem endru ennik kollaadha seyyaar
Thulakkatra kaatchiyavar.
kurals.meaning: People of steady judgement never think ‘the king favours us’ and then do things the king would not accept.
kurals.elementary: Being the teacher’s favourite does not mean you can break the rules. A sensible student knows that being liked is not a free pass, and keeps behaving well so that the trust lasts.
kurals.university: The couplet pivots on two forms of kol (to take, to accept). Kolappattem means ‘we have been accepted or esteemed [by the king]’, and kollaadha means ‘things [he] would not accept’. The echo makes the point that acceptance by the king does not make the unacceptable acceptable. Thulakkatra kaatchi, ‘vision without wavering’, marks the wise courtier as one whose judgement does not drift once favour arrives. Parimelazhagar reads the error as a specific psychology: favour breeds presumption, and presumption breeds offence. That links the couplet forward to 700, where old familiarity replaces present favour as the source of self-deception. The couplet also refines 692: not coveting what is the king’s includes not coveting the licence that favour seems to give.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna promises to pardon a hundred offences from his kinsman Shishupala. Relying on that forbearance, Shishupala heaps insults on Krishna at Yudhishthira’s royal consecration, until the hundredth is passed and he is struck down.
hinduism.explanation: Shishupala treats his protected status as permission to offend, and it ruins him.
hinduism.tie_back: He is the clearest mythic case of the person who thinks ‘I am accepted’ and so does what cannot be accepted.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Shishupala-vadha), trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong illustration of presuming on favour. Shishupala is a rival king, not a courtier, and the favour is a boon rather than royal esteem.

christianity.quote_or_event: “So likewise ye, when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that a servant, however faithful, should claim no special standing from his service.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s steady-minded servant likewise never turns favour into a claim to licence.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the servant’s refusal to presume. It concerns discipleship rather than the politics of a court.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet or be loud to him in speech like the loudness of some of you to others, lest your deeds become worthless while you perceive not.”
islam.explanation: The Quran warns the Prophet’s own companions, the people closest to him, not to become loud or casual in his presence, or their good deeds could be lost without their noticing.
islam.tie_back: Being close to the leader is no licence for improper conduct, which is the Kural’s point about favoured courtiers.
islam._accuracy_note: Good parallel on closeness not excusing disrespect. The setting is the Prophet, not a king.

judaism.quote_or_event: “So Haman came in. And the king said unto him, What shall be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour? Now Haman thought in his heart, To whom would the king delight to do honour more than to myself?”
judaism.explanation: Haman, the Persian king’s favourite, is so sure of his standing that he misreads the king’s question, and his presumption leads to his downfall.
judaism.tie_back: Haman is the Kural’s foolish favourite, whose certainty that he is esteemed blinds his judgement.
judaism._accuracy_note: Vivid narrative match on a favourite’s presumption. Haman’s deeper fault is malice as well as overconfidence.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let him not seat himself on the king’s chair or couch or seat or elephant or chariot; as thinking himself a privileged person, such a one may dwell in a king’s court.”
buddhism.explanation: Vidhura forbids a courtier from taking royal privileges because he believes himself specially favoured.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘Thinking himself a privileged person’ is precisely the Kural’s kolappattem endru enni, thinking ‘we are esteemed’.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near-exact psychological parallel. Dhaumya’s counsel in the Mahabharata has the same rule.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ixion is invited by Zeus to live among the gods on Olympus and is even purified by him. Presuming on this favour, he tries to seduce Hera, and is bound for ever to a turning wheel.
greek_mythology.explanation: Pindar tells the story as the warning of a guest who could not bear his great good fortune.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ixion is the Kural’s favourite who, sure that he is accepted, does the unacceptable.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong parallel of favour leading to presumption and ruin. The offence is sexual transgression rather than general impropriety.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that in friendships between unequals, such as ruler and subject, the lesser party must give more honour and love in proportion. The friendship breaks down when the lesser party forgets the difference.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, a friendship between unequals lasts only if the lower party keeps the proper ratio of honour.
philosophy.tie_back: The favoured courtier who stops honouring the difference because he is ‘accepted’ breaks exactly this proportion.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 8.7 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Offers the theory behind the Kural’s warning. It is abstract and does not describe the favourite’s self-deception.

adhikaram.english: Conduct in the Presence of the King

kurals.tamil:
பழையம் எனக்கருதிப் பண்பல்ல செய்யும்
கெழுதகைமை கேடு தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Pazhaiyam enak karudhip panpalla seyyum
Kezhudhakaimai kedu tharum.
kurals.meaning: The familiarity that makes someone behave improperly because ‘we are old friends of the king’ will bring that person to ruin.
kurals.elementary: Suppose your best friend from kindergarten becomes the class president. If you start bossing them around or ignoring the rules because ‘we go way back’, the friendship and your place will both suffer. Old friendship is precious, but it is not permission to misbehave.
kurals.university: Pazhaiyam means ‘we are old [associates]’, and panpalla are ‘things that are not proper conduct’. The subject of the sentence is kezhudhakaimai, the intimate familiarity, or the privilege claimed through intimacy, that leads to such conduct, and it is this that tharum (brings) kedu (ruin). The word matters because chapter 81 (Pazhaimai, ‘Old Friendship’) uses kezhudhakaimai approvingly for the easy freedom old friends allow each other. Valluvar deliberately shows that the same freedom, turned toward a king, becomes fatal. The chapter thus ends where it began: the right distance from the fire is not closed by long acquaintance. The older text reads “பழைய மெனக்கருதிப் பண்பல்ல செய்யுங் / கெழுதகைமை கேடு தரும்.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: Drona, now poor, goes to King Drupada and greets him as a boyhood friend, reminding him of the promises they made as students. Drupada scornfully replies that friendship between a king and a poor man cannot last, and the insulted Drona later takes revenge.
hinduism.explanation: In the Adi Parva, Drona treats old intimacy as a claim on a reigning king, and the encounter ends in humiliation and lasting enmity.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s pazhaiyam, ‘we are old friends’, presumed upon before a throne, with ruin following for both men.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava sub-parva (Drona and Drupada), trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong parallel on presuming on old friendship with a king. The epic arguably blames Drupada’s arrogance as much as Drona’s presumption.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A prophet is not without honour, but in his own country, and among his own kin, and in his own house.”
christianity.explanation: In his home town, people who have known Jesus since childhood dismiss him because of their familiarity with his family.
christianity.tie_back: The same force the Kural warns about is at work: long familiarity erodes proper reverence.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shows how familiarity breeds disrespect, but from the side of the one disrespected, and with no ruin befalling the familiar.

islam.quote_or_event: “Do not make [your] calling of the Messenger among yourselves as the call of one of you to another.”
islam.explanation: The Quran tells the believers, many of them the Prophet’s long-time companions, not to address him as casually as they address one another.
islam.tie_back: Long companionship does not license casual treatment of the one in authority, which is the Kural’s warning against kezhudhakaimai.
islam._accuracy_note: Close parallel on familiarity toward a leader. The verse goes on to warn of trial or punishment, matching the Kural’s ‘ruin’.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Withdraw thy foot from thy neighbour’s house; lest he be weary of thee, and so hate thee.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs warns that visiting too often turns welcome into weariness and even hatred.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts teach that intimacy pushed too far destroys the relationship it relies on.
judaism._accuracy_note: General wisdom on overfamiliarity. It is about a neighbour, not a king.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Channa, the Buddha’s charioteer from his days as a prince, grows arrogant because of that old bond and treats other monks with contempt. Before his death the Buddha orders the ‘higher penalty’ (brahmadanda): the monks are simply not to speak to him. Channa is shaken into humility.
buddhism.explanation: Channa’s pride rests on his old closeness to the Buddha, and it earns him a formal penalty from the Buddha himself.
buddhism.tie_back: Channa is the Buddhist model of the Kural’s pazhaiyam enak karudhi: presuming on old intimacy, followed by consequences.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta 6.4; background in Vinaya commentarial tradition
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good parallel. The detail about Channa’s arrogance from old intimacy comes from the Vinaya and commentaries rather than DN 16 itself.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Tantalus, a mortal favoured to dine at the gods’ own table, abuses that intimacy by stealing their nectar and ambrosia for his mortal friends. His punishment is eternal hunger and thirst, with food and water always just out of reach.
greek_mythology.explanation: Pindar says Tantalus could not digest his great good fortune and turned the gods’ closeness into offence.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Tantalus turned intimacy with the highest powers into improper liberties, which is exactly the kezhudhakaimai that brings ruin.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong parallel of intimacy with the powerful abused and punished. Pindar rejects the harsher cannibalism version of the myth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “… who with his own hand while at table stabbed Clitus, his dearest friend, who had been brought up with him, because he did not flatter him enough, and was too slow in transforming himself from a free man and a Macedonian into a Persian slave.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca recalls how Alexander killed Clitus, a friend he had grown up with, at a banquet for speaking too freely, and how he caged Lysimachus, another close friend, with a lion.
philosophy.tie_back: Clitus' fate shows the Kural's warning in action: an old intimacy with a king did not protect the friend who took liberties in his presence, and it led to his ruin.
philosophy.source: Seneca, De Ira (Of Anger), III.17 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Wikisource (Stewart translation, Book III). Next-best partial match: the event fits the Kural closely, but Seneca condemns Alexander's anger rather than Clitus' over-familiarity, so the moral is drawn from the opposite side.
